title: Controlled Dark-State Energy Storage and Work Extraction in V-Type Quantum Batteries
abstract: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on its ability to retain stored energy against unwanted discharge but also on the amount of useful work that can be extracted from it. Here, we investigate these complementary aspects in an ensemble of V-type qutrits coupled to a lossy cavity. By applying a finite splitting pulse to the two excited states of each qutrit, cavity-bright excitations are converted into atomic dark states, whose populations remain protected upon restoring degeneracy, even while the light-matter coupling remains active. Simulations with finite-duration pulses reveal a capture window governed by the competition among energy transfer, bright-to-dark conversion, and photon leakage. We further show that if the energy is stored in the fully symmetric atomic subspace, the passive energy is bounded by twice the transition energy for number of atoms $N\geq2$. Consequently, if the stored energy scales extensively with $N$, the ratio of extractable work to stored energy approaches unity in the thermodynamic limit. Comparing different initial preparations at equal mean input energy, we find that coherent-state can yield greater finite-time ergotropy despite capturing less energy, whereas Fock-state favors greater extractable work in the stationary component. Our results demonstrate how controlled dark-state population trapping in an atom-cavity coupled system can protect stored energy while providing a conditional route toward high extractable work.
summary: This paper analyzes a quantum battery using V-type qutrits coupled to a cavity, focusing on protecting stored energy via dark-state population trapping. By controlling the system dynamics with tailored pulses, the authors demonstrate a pathway to extract useful work efficiently. The results highlight a trade-off between initial state preparation (coherent vs. Fock) and the type of extractable work measured (finite-time vs. stationary).
main_problem: The paper investigates the controlled storage of energy and the subsequent extraction of useful work from a quantum battery system.
main_result: Controlled dark-state population trapping protects stored energy, and the extractable work can approach the stored energy in the thermodynamic limit.
method: The study uses theoretical simulations solving the Lindblad master equation to model the time evolution of the coupled atom-cavity system.
model_or_system: The system consists of an ensemble of N V-type qutrits coupled to a lossy cavity, described by a Hamiltonian including cavity, atomic, and interaction terms, and evolving under dissipation.
key_observables: Atomic energy ($E_a$), passive energy ($E_{	ext{pass}}$), ergotropy ($E$), and protected dark-state population ($\langle \hat{N}_D angle$).
important_parameters: The number of atoms ($N$), cavity loss rate ($\kappa$), and the strength/duration of the splitting pulse ($\delta(t)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes Markovian dissipation and relies on symmetry arguments (excited-state exchange and ensemble permutation) to derive energy bounds.
figures_summary: Figures compare energy, passive energy, and ergotropy for coherent vs. Fock initial states, showing differences between finite-time and stationary work extraction.
paper_structure: The paper develops the model, details the dark-state storage protocol using controlled pulses, analyzes the energy bounds based on symmetry, and compares the performance of different initial state preparations (coherent vs. Fock) for work extraction.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses fundamental questions in open quantum systems, specifically how controlled coherent dynamics can protect quantum resources (energy) against dissipation while enabling high-efficiency work extraction.
